title: How schools mask poor writing
author: Mark Enser
summary: In Part Seven of his Supporting Unwilling Writers series, Mark Enser examines well-meant school habits that make writing look better while hiding the underlying problem. Writing frames, sentence starters and templates such as PEE help struggling pupils at first, but when support never comes off, or when the template becomes the target that leaders check in book scrutiny, pupils can reproduce the form without the thinking. He cites Ofsted's review of English, which found weaknesses masked by narrow approaches, and Wray and Lewis's original advice that frames should be used less and less. He adds that no single master frame can serve the ten kinds of writing geographers do, that extended writing demanded before knowledge is secure only hides the gap, and that heavy marking can teach pupils that attempting is risky. His eight-step remedy includes planning the fade, testing pupils without the frame, teaching the move before the words, keeping structures out of accountability and marking less but better, and he shares a geography writing framework with Somerset Levels examples.
points: Scaffolds help only if they are planned to fade, and research on expertise reversal shows prompts that stay in place eventually get in the way.
When a structure appears on displays, success criteria and book looks it stops being a tool and becomes the target, so pupils can hit it without thinking geographically.
Writing varies by discipline and purpose, so one whole-school frame for extended writing distorts most of the kinds of writing it is applied to.
A simple diagnostic is to set a task with no frame and compare it to supported work, or to notice when thirty answers start identically.
Progress in writing should mean more precise links between ideas, not longer sentences, and marking should focus on one error type at a time.
quotes: A pupil can hit the target, with a point, some evidence and an explanation, without having thought geographically at all. The writing looks right. The thinking may not be there.

Ofsted’s review of English teaching found that, for pupils who struggle with writing, “laptops, writing frames and short responses often replace opportunities for pupils to work on the specific knowledge and skills they need support with.

A structure is introduced to help. It appears on a slide, then on a display, then in the success criteria. Before long it’s on the book scrutiny form, and teachers are being asked whether pupils are using it.
Sentence starters work the same way, with an extra catch: they shape the thought as well as the sentence.

When pupils are asked for an extended answer before they know enough to write one, a frame gets something onto the page anyway. The book fills up. The gap in knowledge stays hidden until there’s no frame to hide behind.

Every few weeks, set a short task with no frame, no starters and no model on the board. Compare it with the supported work in their books. If the two look very different, the frame has been doing the thinking.
The question to ask of a beautiful paragraph isn’t whether it looks right. It’s whether the pupil could have written it without the frame.
